questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a property that distinguishes a liquid from a gas?
options: A gas fills any container completely
A liquid has a free surface
A gas is far more compressible
A liquid has a fixed volume

options: air molecules stop moving when squeezed
questions.explanation: Gas molecules have large spaces between them which can be reduced; liquid molecules are already in near contact.

questions.explanation: The kelvin (temperature) is one of the seven S.I. base units; the others listed are derived units.

questions.stem: Which of the following lists contains only fundamental quantities?
questions.explanation: Speed, force, density and charge are derived; mass, time and amount of substance are base quantities.

questions.explanation: Work = force x distance = (kg m s^-2)(m) = kg m^2 s^-2. kg m s^-2 is the newton; kg m^2 s^-3 is the watt.

questions.explanation: Momentum = mass x velocity = M x L T^-1.

Its displacement is zero but its distance is not
Its distance and displacement are both zero
Its displacement equals the reading of its odometer
Its distance is a vector quantity

questions.stem: The S.I. unit of time is defined in terms of
options: the swing of a seconds pendulum
the radiation of the caesium-133 atom
the flow of sand in an hourglass
questions.explanation: The second is defined from a fixed frequency of the radiation from the caesium-133 atom.

upthrust in sea water is greater than the weight
sea water has a lower surface tension
sea water is denser than fresh water
fresh water is denser than sea water
questions.explanation: The upthrust must equal the same weight in both; the denser sea water needs a smaller displaced volume.

questions.explanation: Smoke particles show irregular zig-zag (Brownian) movement, which is random motion.

questions.stem: A vector is represented graphically by

a line drawn to scale with an arrow-head
a line of any length without direction
questions.explanation: The length (to scale) gives the magnitude and the arrow-head gives the direction.

questions.explanation: 60 x (50 - 15) = 70 x d gives d = 30 cm from the pivot, i.e. the 80 cm mark.

questions.stem: A loaded lorry is most stable when its
options: centre of gravity is high and base is wide
centre of gravity is high and base is narrow
centre of gravity is low and base is wide
load is placed on the roof

questions.explanation: Solar energy is continually replenished; fossil fuels and uranium are finite.

chemical energy of coal into electrical energy

questions.topic: Measurement of electric current, p.d., resistance, e.m.f. and internal resistance of a cell
questions.stem: The potentiometer is preferred to a voltmeter for measuring the e.m.f. of a cell because at balance it
options: draws no current from the cell
questions.explanation: At balance no current flows through the cell, so there is no lost volts and the true e.m.f. is measured.

questions.topic: Properties of magnets and magnetic materials
questions.stem: The only sure test that a steel bar is a magnet is
options: it being heavier than an unmagnetised bar
questions.explanation: Attraction happens between a magnet and any magnetic material; repulsion occurs only between like poles of two magnets.

questions.stem: A student wants to destroy the magnetism of an old steel bar magnet. The best method is to
options: heat it to red heat and let it cool lying east-west
stroke it repeatedly with a strong magnet
put it inside a coil carrying direct current
questions.explanation: Strong heating agitates the domains into random directions; cooling east-west avoids remagnetisation by the earth's field.

questions.stem: A neutral point in the field of a bar magnet placed with its north pole pointing to geographic north is located
options: at the north pole of the magnet
at the centre of the magnet
at the south pole of the magnet
on the east-west axis of the magnet
on the axis beyond the north pole
questions.explanation: With N pointing north, the magnet's field opposes the earth's field on the equatorial (east-west) line, giving neutral points there.

questions.topic: Magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor and between parallel conductors
questions.stem: A conductor 0.25 m long carries 8 A at 30 degrees to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. The force on it is
questions.explanation: F = BIl sin theta = 0.5 x 8 x 0.25 x 0.5 = 0.5 N.

questions.topic: Magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor and between parallel conductors
questions.stem: Two parallel overhead cables carry currents in opposite directions. The force between them is
options: perpendicular to both cables and the line joining them
questions.explanation: Antiparallel currents repel; parallel currents attract.

questions.stem: The core of an electromagnet is made of soft iron because soft iron
options: is a poor conductor of electricity
questions.explanation: Soft iron loses its magnetism when the current is switched off, which is needed in bells, relays and cranes.

questions.stem: The angle between the magnetic meridian and the geographic meridian at a place is the
questions.explanation: Declination (variation) is the angle between magnetic north and true north.

questions.topic: Magnetic force on a moving charged particle

questions.explanation: Lenz's law follows from the conservation of energy.

questions.explanation: E = N Delta phi/Delta t = 200 x 0.05/0.25 = 40 V.

questions.explanation: Thin insulated laminations increase the resistance to eddy currents in the core.

questions.explanation: Ip = Vs Is/Vp = 12 x 4/240 = 0.2 A.

options: lags behind the voltage by a quarter of a cycle
is in phase with the voltage
is half a cycle ahead of the voltage
leads the voltage by a quarter of a cycle
questions.explanation: In a pure inductor the current lags the voltage by 90 degrees (a quarter cycle).

questions.explanation: Power factor = P/(V I) = 288/(240 x 2) = 0.6.

questions.stem: In Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment, the fact that most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil showed that
options: the atom is a solid sphere
the atom is mostly empty space
electrons are spread through the atom
questions.explanation: Most particles were undeflected because the atom is mostly empty space, with its mass in a tiny nucleus.

questions.stem: The atomic model described as a 'plum pudding' was proposed by
questions.explanation: Thomson pictured electrons embedded in a sphere of positive charge.

questions.stem: An electron in a hydrogen atom falls from the level of energy -3.4 eV to the level of energy -13.6 eV. The wavelength of the photon emitted is (h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s, c = 3.0 x 10^8 m s^-1, 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J)
questions.explanation: Energy = 10.2 eV = 1.632e-18 J; lambda = hc/E = 1.98e-25/1.632e-18 = 1.21 x 10^-7 m (ultraviolet).

questions.stem: Electrons are emitted from a caesium surface with maximum kinetic energy 0.9 eV when light of photon energy 2.8 eV falls on it. The work function of caesium is
In the photoelectric effect, increasing the intensity of the incident light (above threshold frequency) increases the
options: number of electrons emitted per second
maximum kinetic energy of the electrons
questions.explanation: More photons per second release more electrons, but each photon's energy, and so the maximum K.E., is unchanged.

questions.stem: The emission of electrons from a heated metal surface is called
questions.explanation: Heating gives electrons enough energy to escape from the surface.

questions.stem: In an X-ray tube, the hardness (penetrating power) of the X-rays is increased by
questions.explanation: Higher accelerating voltage gives electrons more energy, producing higher-frequency (harder) X-rays.

questions.stem: The target in an X-ray tube is usually made of tungsten because tungsten has a
questions.explanation: Most of the electron energy becomes heat in the target, so a metal with a very high melting point is needed.

questions.stem: A nuclide is represented as 238/92 U (mass number 238, atomic number 92). The number of neutrons in its nucleus is
questions.explanation: Neutrons = 238 - 92 = 146.

questions.stem: Thorium-234 (proton number 90) decays by beta emission. The proton number and nucleon number of the daughter nucleus are
questions.explanation: Beta emission raises the proton number by 1 and leaves the nucleon number unchanged.

questions.stem: A radioactive sample has a half-life of 6 days. The fraction remaining after 24 days is
questions.explanation: 24 days = 4 half-lives, so the fraction left is (1/2)^4 = 1/16.

questions.stem: The activity of a sample falls from 640 counts per minute to 40 counts per minute in 20 hours. Its half-life is
questions.explanation: 640 to 40 is a factor of 16 = 2^4, so 4 half-lives in 20 h: half-life = 5 h.

questions.stem: Which of the following radiations is deflected most by a magnetic field?
questions.explanation: Beta particles have a very small mass and so are deflected most; gamma rays, X-rays and neutrons are not deflected.

questions.stem: The source of the sun's energy is
questions.explanation: In the sun hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, releasing energy.

questions.stem: When a beam of electrons is passed through a thin graphite film, rings similar to those of X-ray diffraction appear on a screen. This is evidence that electrons
questions.explanation: Diffraction rings are a wave effect, confirming de Broglie's prediction of matter waves.

questions.stem: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of momentum 3.3 x 10^-24 kg m s^-1 is (h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s)
Which of the following phenomena is best explained by treating light as a stream of particles?
questions.explanation: The photoelectric effect needs light energy to be delivered in packets (photons).

questions.stem: A stone is thrown horizontally at 15 m s^-1 from the top of a cliff 45 m high. The time taken to reach the ground is (g = 10 m s^-2)
questions.explanation: Vertical motion: 45 = 0.5 x 10 x t^2, t = 3 s.

questions.explanation: R = u^2 sin 2 theta/g = 400 x sin 60/10 = 34.6 m.

questions.stem: At the highest point of the path of a projectile, its
questions.explanation: The vertical component is momentarily zero; the horizontal component remains, and the acceleration is still g.

questions.stem: A geostationary communication satellite such as NigComSat-1R has an orbital period of about
questions.explanation: A geostationary satellite orbits once per day, staying above a fixed point on the equator.

questions.stem: A satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius 7.0 x 10^6 m where the acceleration due to gravity is 8.0 m s^-2. Its orbital speed is
questions.explanation: v = sqrt(g r) = sqrt(8 x 7e6) = 7483 m s^-1 = 7.5 km s^-1.

questions.stem: Astronauts in an orbiting spacecraft feel weightless because
options: they and the spacecraft are falling freely together
the spacecraft shields them from gravity
there is no gravity in space
questions.explanation: Both are in free fall towards the earth, so there is no contact force on the astronauts.

questions.stem: A spring of force constant 400 N m^-1 is stretched by 5 cm. The force applied is
A copper wire 3.0 m long with cross-sectional area 1.5 x 10^-6 m^2 is stretched by a force of 60 N. If Young's modulus for copper is 1.2 x 10^11 Pa, the extension is
The work done in stretching a spring of force constant 300 N m^-1 by 0.2 m is
The point beyond which a wire does not return to its original length when the load is removed is the
questions.explanation: Beyond the elastic limit, deformation is permanent (plastic).

questions.stem: A cooking pot is made of aluminium with a wooden handle because
options: aluminium conducts heat well and wood conducts poorly
aluminium has a high specific heat capacity
aluminium is a poor conductor of heat
wood is a good conductor of heat
questions.explanation: The pot transfers heat quickly to the food while the poorly conducting handle stays cool.

questions.stem: Heat flows through a copper slab 0.02 m thick and 0.5 m^2 in area whose faces are at 80 degrees C and 30 degrees C. If the thermal conductivity of copper is 400 W m^-1 K^-1, the rate of heat flow is
questions.explanation: Q/t = kA Delta theta/x = 400 x 0.5 x 50/0.02 = 5.0 x 10^5 W.

questions.stem: Light is kept inside an optical fibre by
questions.explanation: Light meets the core-cladding boundary at angles greater than the critical angle and is totally internally reflected.

questions.stem: For total internal reflection in an optical fibre, the cladding must have
options: a higher refractive index than the core
a lower refractive index than the core
the same refractive index as the core
questions.explanation: TIR only happens when light travels towards a medium of lower refractive index.

questions.stem: In the word LASER, the letter S stands for
questions.explanation: LASER means Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation.

questions.stem: Laser light is used for delicate eye surgery mainly because it
options: is a narrow, intense, coherent beam that can be focused precisely
contains every colour of the spectrum
questions.explanation: A laser beam is monochromatic, coherent and highly directional, so it can be focused to a tiny, intense spot.

questions.stem: A bismuth rod suspended between the poles of a strong magnet sets itself at right angles to the field because bismuth is
questions.explanation: Diamagnetic materials are weakly repelled, so the rod turns across the field.

questions.stem: Steel rather than soft iron is used for making permanent magnets because steel
questions.explanation: Steel has a high retentivity and coercivity, so it keeps its magnetism.

questions.stem: An example of a semiconductor is
questions.explanation: Silicon and germanium are the common semiconductors.

questions.stem: In a p-type semiconductor, the majority charge carriers are
questions.explanation: Doping with a trivalent element creates holes, which are the majority carriers in p-type material.

questions.stem: A p-n junction diode is used in a circuit mainly to
questions.explanation: A diode conducts in one direction only, converting a.c. to d.c.

questions.stem: As the temperature of a pure semiconductor is raised, its resistance
questions.explanation: More electron-hole pairs are produced as temperature rises, so conductivity increases and resistance falls.

questions.topic: Structure of matter (kinetic theory and diffusion)
questions.stem: Hydrogen diffuses faster than oxygen at the same temperature because hydrogen molecules
options: have a smaller mass and so move faster
questions.explanation: At the same temperature both have the same average K.E., so the lighter hydrogen molecules move faster.

questions.topic: Structure of matter (kinetic theory and diffusion)
questions.stem: The rise of water in a narrow glass tube is due to
options: atmospheric pressure pushing down the water
questions.explanation: Water molecules are attracted more strongly to glass than to one another, so water wets the glass and rises (capillarity).

questions.stem:
(a) State Archimedes' principle. [2 marks]
(b) Explain why a steel ship floats although steel is denser than water. [2 marks]
(c) A rectangular plastic water tank of length 0.6 m, width 0.4 m and height 0.2 m has a mass of 30 kg. It is placed upright in a fishpond. (Density of water = 1000 kg m^-3, g = 10 m s^-2.)
(i) Calculate the weight of the tank. [2 marks]
(ii) Calculate the depth to which the tank sinks when it floats. [4 marks]
(iii) Calculate the upthrust on the tank when it is pushed down until it is just completely submerged (water not entering it). [3 marks]
(iv) Hence find the extra downward force needed to hold it in this position. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) When a body is wholly or partially immersed in a fluid it experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of fluid displaced
2 marks: (b) The hull is hollow, so it displaces a large volume of water whose weight equals the ship's weight before it is fully submerged (average density of ship less than water)
1 mark: (c)(i) W = mg = 30 x 10
1 mark: = 300 N
1 mark: (c)(ii) Floating: upthrust = weight = 300 N
1 mark: Volume displaced = 300/(1000 x 10) = 0.030 m^3
1 mark: Base area = 0.6 x 0.4 = 0.24 m^2
1 mark: Depth = 0.030/0.24 = 0.125 m (12.5 cm)
1 mark: (c)(iii) Volume of tank = 0.6 x 0.4 x 0.2 = 0.048 m^3
2 marks: Upthrust = 0.048 x 1000 x 10 = 480 N
2 marks: (c)(iv) Extra force = 480 - 300 = 180 N
questions.explanation: (a) Upthrust equals weight of fluid displaced. (b) Hollow hull displaces enough water. (c) W = 300 N; floating depth = 300/(1000 x 10 x 0.24) = 0.125 m; full upthrust = 480 N; extra force 180 N.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between static friction and dynamic (sliding) friction. [2 marks]
(b) State two laws of solid friction. [2 marks]
(c) A crate of mass 25 kg rests on a rough plank inclined at 30 degrees to the horizontal at a loading bay in Apapa. The coefficient of sliding friction between crate and plank is 0.2. (g = 10 m s^-2)
(i) Calculate the component of the weight of the crate acting down the plank. [2 marks]
(ii) Calculate the normal reaction and the sliding friction. [3 marks]
(iii) Calculate the force parallel to the plank needed to push the crate up the plank at constant speed. [3 marks]
(iv) If the crate is released and slides down, calculate its acceleration. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) Static friction: the force that opposes the start of motion between surfaces at rest relative to each other
1 mark: Dynamic friction: the force opposing motion when one surface is already sliding over the other (it is slightly less than limiting static friction)
2 marks: (b) Any two: friction opposes relative motion; is independent of area of contact; is proportional to the normal reaction; depends on the nature of the surfaces; dynamic friction is independent of speed (1 mark each)
1 mark: (c)(i) mg sin 30 = 25 x 10 x 0.5
1 mark: = 125 N
1 mark: (c)(ii) R = mg cos 30 = 250 x 0.866 = 216.5 N
1 mark: F = mu R = 0.2 x 216.5
1 mark: = 43.3 N
2 marks: (c)(iii) Force = mg sin 30 + F = 125 + 43.3
1 mark: = 168.3 N
1 mark: (c)(iv) Net force down the plank = 125 - 43.3 = 81.7 N
2 marks: a = 81.7/25 = 3.27 m s^-2
questions.explanation: Down-slope component 125 N; R = 216.5 N; friction 43.3 N; push up at steady speed = 168.3 N; sliding down a = 81.7/25 = 3.27 m s^-2.

questions.topic: Equations of motion with constant acceleration
questions.stem:
(a) Write down the three equations of uniformly accelerated motion, defining each symbol. [3 marks]
(b) A BRT bus starts from rest at a bus stop and accelerates uniformly at 2.5 m s^-2 for 8 s. It then moves at constant velocity for 12 s before the driver brakes, producing a uniform deceleration of 4 m s^-2 until it stops.
(i) Calculate the maximum velocity reached. [2 marks]
(ii) Calculate the time taken during braking. [2 marks]
(iii) Calculate the total distance travelled. [5 marks]
(iv) Calculate the average speed for the whole journey. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) v = u + at; s = ut + (1/2)at^2; v^2 = u^2 + 2as, where u = initial velocity, v = final velocity, a = acceleration, t = time, s = displacement (1 mark per equation with symbols)
1 mark: (b)(i) v = u + at = 0 + 2.5 x 8
1 mark: = 20 m s^-1
1 mark: (b)(ii) t = (v - u)/a = 20/4
1 mark: = 5 s
1 mark: (b)(iii) First stage: s = (1/2) x 2.5 x 8^2 = 80 m
1 mark: Second stage: s = 20 x 12 = 240 m
2 marks: Third stage: s = v^2/(2a) = 400/8 = 50 m
1 mark: Total distance = 370 m
1 mark: (b)(iv) Total time = 8 + 12 + 5 = 25 s
2 marks: Average speed = 370/25 = 14.8 m s^-1
questions.explanation: (b) v max = 20 m s^-1; braking time 5 s; distances 80 + 240 + 50 = 370 m; total time 25 s; average speed 14.8 m s^-1.

questions.stem:
(a) State the principle of moments. [2 marks]
(b) Define the moment of a force about a point and state its S.I. unit. [2 marks]
(c) A uniform metre rule of mass 120 g is pivoted at the 40 cm mark and is balanced horizontally by hanging a mass M at the 10 cm mark.
(i) Name the forces acting on the rule and state where each acts. [2 marks]
(ii) Calculate M. [4 marks]
(d) A non-uniform rod of mass 120 g balances on a knife-edge at its 45 cm mark when a 30 g mass hangs at its 5 cm mark. Calculate the position of the centre of gravity of the rod. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) When a body is in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about the same point
1 mark: (b) Moment = force x perpendicular distance of its line of action from the point
1 mark: Unit: newton metre (N m)
2 marks: (c)(i) Weight of rule (120 g) acting at the 50 cm mark, 10 cm right of pivot; M at 10 cm mark, 30 cm left of pivot; upward reaction at the pivot (40 cm)
2 marks: (c)(ii) Taking moments about pivot: M x (40 - 10) = 120 x (50 - 40)
1 mark: 30M = 1200
1 mark: M = 40 g
1 mark: (d) The 30 g mass is 45 - 5 = 40 cm from the knife-edge (anticlockwise moment = 30 x 40 = 1200 g cm)
1 mark: The centre of gravity must lie on the other side of the knife-edge at distance d
2 marks: 120 x d = 1200, so d = 10 cm
1 mark: Centre of gravity at the 55 cm mark
questions.explanation: (c) M x 30 = 120 x 10 gives M = 40 g. (d) 30 x 40 = 120 d, d = 10 cm, so the centre of gravity is at the 55 cm mark.

questions.topic: Period, frequency and amplitude of S.H.M.
questions.stem:
(a) Define the following terms as applied to simple harmonic motion: (i) amplitude; (ii) period; (iii) frequency. [3 marks]
(b) State two examples of simple harmonic motion in everyday life. [2 marks]
(c) A simple pendulum of length 1.6 m oscillates with amplitude 5.0 cm at a place where g = 10 m s^-2. Calculate:
(i) the period; [3 marks]
(ii) the frequency; [2 marks]
(iii) the angular velocity (angular frequency); [2 marks]
(iv) the maximum speed of the bob. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a)(i) Amplitude: maximum displacement from the equilibrium position
1 mark: (ii) Period: time for one complete oscillation
1 mark: (iii) Frequency: number of complete oscillations per second
2 marks: (b) Any two: swinging pendulum of a clock; vibrating guitar string; loaded spring bobbing; vibrating tuning fork prong; oscillating loaded test tube in water (1 mark each)
1 mark: (c)(i) T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g) = 2 pi sqrt(1.6/10)
1 mark: = 2 pi x 0.4
1 mark: = 2.51 s
1 mark: (c)(ii) f = 1/T = 1/2.51
1 mark: = 0.40 Hz
1 mark: (c)(iii) w = 2 pi/T = sqrt(g/l)
1 mark: = 2.5 rad s^-1
1 mark: (c)(iv) v max = w A
1 mark: = 2.5 x 0.050
1 mark: = 0.125 m s^-1

questions.topic: Second Law: force, acceleration, momentum and impulse
questions.stem:
(a) State Newton's second law of motion. [2 marks]
(b) Show from the law that F = ma, stating any assumption made. [3 marks]
(c) A car of mass 1500 kg travelling at 20 m s^-1 runs into the back of a stationary car of mass 1000 kg on the Lagos-Ibadan expressway. The two cars lock together after the collision.
(i) Calculate their common velocity just after the collision. [3 marks]
(ii) Calculate the loss of kinetic energy in the collision. [4 marks]
(iii) If the impact lasted 0.40 s, calculate the average force exerted on the stationary car. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the resultant force acting on it and takes place in the direction of the force
1 mark: (b) F is proportional to (mv - mu)/t
1 mark: With constant mass, F is proportional to m(v - u)/t = ma
1 mark: With the unit of force (newton) chosen so that the constant is 1, F = ma
1 mark: (c)(i) Total momentum before = 1500 x 20 + 0 = 30 000 kg m s^-1
1 mark: (1500 + 1000) v = 30 000
1 mark: v = 12 m s^-1
1 mark: (c)(ii) K.E. before = 0.5 x 1500 x 20^2 = 300 000 J
1 mark: K.E. after = 0.5 x 2500 x 12^2 = 180 000 J
2 marks: Loss = 300 000 - 180 000 = 120 000 J (1.2 x 10^5 J)
1 mark: (c)(iii) Change in momentum of stationary car = 1000 x 12 = 12 000 kg m s^-1
2 marks: F = 12 000/0.40 = 30 000 N (3.0 x 10^4 N)
questions.explanation: Common velocity 12 m s^-1; K.E. loss 300 000 - 180 000 = 120000 J; force on the stationary car = 12 000/0.40 = 30000 N.

questions.stem:
(a) Define (i) mechanical advantage; (ii) velocity ratio; (iii) efficiency of a machine. [3 marks]
(b) Explain why the efficiency of a pulley system is always less than 100%. [2 marks]
(c) A block-and-tackle pulley system with a velocity ratio of 5 is used on a building site to raise a load of 900 N through a height of 2.0 m. The effort applied is 250 N. Calculate:
(i) the mechanical advantage; [2 marks]
(ii) the efficiency; [2 marks]
(iii) the work done on the load; [2 marks]
(iv) the work done by the effort; [2 marks]
(v) the energy wasted. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a)(i) M.A. = load/effort
1 mark: (ii) V.R. = distance moved by effort/distance moved by load
1 mark: (iii) Efficiency = work output/work input x 100%
2 marks: (b) Some of the work input is wasted in overcoming friction at the pulley bearings and in lifting the lower (movable) pulley block and rope
1 mark: (c)(i) M.A. = 900/250
1 mark: = 3.6
1 mark: (c)(ii) Efficiency = 3.6/5 x 100%
1 mark: = 72%
1 mark: (c)(iii) Work output = 900 x 2.0
1 mark: = 1800 J
1 mark: (c)(iv) Effort distance = 5 x 2.0 = 10 m; work input = 250 x 10
1 mark: = 2500 J
1 mark: (c)(v) Energy wasted = 2500 - 1800
1 mark: = 700 J
questions.explanation: M.A. = 3.6; efficiency = 72%; work output 1800 J; work input 2500 J; energy wasted 700 J.

questions.stem:
(a) Define specific latent heat of fusion. [2 marks]
(b) Using the kinetic theory, explain why the temperature of melting ice remains constant although heat is being supplied. [3 marks]
(c) A 500 W electric heater is used to melt 0.20 kg of ice at 0 degrees C and then to heat the resulting water to 100 degrees C. Assuming no heat is lost, calculate:
(i) the heat required to melt the ice; [2 marks]
(ii) the time taken to melt the ice; [2 marks]
(iii) the heat required to raise the water from 0 degrees C to 100 degrees C; [2 marks]
(iv) the time taken for this heating. [2 marks]
(d) State one reason why the actual time taken would be longer. [2 marks]
[Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1; specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The quantity of heat required to change unit mass (1 kg) of a substance from solid to liquid at its melting point without change of temperature
3 marks: (b) The heat supplied is used to break the bonds/overcome the intermolecular forces holding the molecules in fixed positions (1); it increases the potential energy, not the average kinetic energy, of the molecules (1); since temperature depends on average K.E., it remains constant (1)
1 mark: (c)(i) Q = mL = 0.20 x 3.36 x 10^5
1 mark: = 6.72 x 10^4 J (67 200 J)
1 mark: (c)(ii) t = Q/P = 67 200/500
1 mark: = 134.4 s
1 mark: (c)(iii) Q = mc Delta theta = 0.20 x 4200 x 100
1 mark: = 84 000 J
1 mark: (c)(iv) t = 84 000/500
1 mark: = 168 s
2 marks: (d) Heat is lost to the surroundings and to the container (any one valid reason)
questions.explanation: Melting needs 67 200 J, taking 134.4 s; heating to 100 degrees C needs 84 000 J, taking 168 s. Heat losses make the actual times longer.

questions.stem:
(a) State (i) Charles' law; (ii) the pressure law. [4 marks]
(b) Explain, using the kinetic theory, why the pressure of a gas in a closed vessel rises when it is heated. [3 marks]
(c) A bicycle pump contains 400 cm^3 of air at a pressure of 1.0 x 10^5 Pa and temperature 27 degrees C. The air is compressed to 300 cm^3 and its temperature rises to 87 degrees C.
(i) Write down the general gas equation. [2 marks]
(ii) Calculate the new pressure of the air. [4 marks]
(iii) State one assumption made in the calculation. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) The volume of a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure is directly proportional to its absolute temperature
2 marks: (a)(ii) The pressure of a fixed mass of gas at constant volume is directly proportional to its absolute temperature
3 marks: (b) Heating increases the average kinetic energy (speed) of the molecules (1); they collide with the walls more frequently (1) and with greater force/momentum change, so pressure increases (1)
2 marks: (c)(i) p1V1/T1 = p2V2/T2 (temperatures in kelvin)
1 mark: (c)(ii) T1 = 300 K, T2 = 360 K
1 mark: p2 = p1 V1 T2/(V2 T1)
1 mark: = 1.0 x 10^5 x 400 x 360/(300 x 300)

1 mark: = 0.68 m

1 mark: = 348 m s^-1

1 mark: = 71 Hz

questions.topic: Period, frequency and amplitude of S.H.M.
questions.stem:
In an experiment to determine the force constant k of a spiral spring, a student suspended the spring from a clamp and attached a mass hanger to its lower end. For each total mass m on the spring, the mass was pulled down slightly and released, and the time t for 20 complete oscillations was measured. The readings were: m/kg: 0.050, 0.100, 0.150, 0.200, 0.250, 0.300; t/s: 7.5, 9.7, 11.6, 13.1, 14.6, 15.9.
(a)(i) Calculate the period T for each mass. [3 marks]
(ii) Calculate T^2 for each mass. [3 marks]
(iii) A graph of T^2 (vertical axis) against m (horizontal axis) gives a best-fit straight line passing through (0.050 kg, 0.138 s^2) and (0.300 kg, 0.630 s^2). Calculate the slope s of the line. [3 marks]
(iv) Given that T^2 = (4 pi^2/k) m + constant, use your slope to determine k. [3 marks]
(v) State two precautions taken to obtain accurate results. [2 marks]
(vi) Why is the time for 20 oscillations measured rather than for one oscillation? [2 marks]
(b)(i) Define simple harmonic motion. [2 marks]
(ii) The same spring is used to support a mass of 0.40 kg. Using your value of k and neglecting the mass of the spring, calculate the period of oscillation. [3 marks]
(iii) State Hooke's law and use your value of k to find the extension produced by a load of 2.0 N. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) T = t/20: 0.375, 0.485, 0.580, 0.655, 0.730, 0.795 s (deduct 1 mark for each wrong value, minimum 0)
3 marks: (a)(ii) T^2: 0.141, 0.235, 0.336, 0.429, 0.533, 0.632 s^2 (deduct 1 mark for each wrong value)

2 marks: = 1.97 s^2 kg^-1 (value 1, unit 1)
1 mark: (a)(iv) k = 4 pi^2/s
2 marks: = 39.48/1.97 = 20.1 N m^-1 (accept 19.1 to 21.1)

2 marks: (b)(i) Motion in which the acceleration is proportional to the displacement from a fixed point and always directed towards that point
1 mark: (b)(ii) T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k)
2 marks: = 2 pi sqrt(0.40/20.1) = 0.89 s

questions.stem:
A spiral spring hangs vertically beside a vertical metre rule. A pointer attached to the lower end of the spring reads 10.8 cm when no load is attached. Loads W were added in turn and the pointer readings R recorded as follows: W/N: 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0; R/cm: 12.4, 13.9, 15.5, 17.1, 18.6, 20.2.

(ii) Calculate the energy stored in the spring when the load is 3.0 N, using your force constant. [3 marks]

1 mark: (b)(i) The sum of upward forces equals the sum of downward forces
1 mark: The sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about that point
2 marks: (b)(ii) Moments about left support: R_right x 6.0 = 450 x 2.0 + 300 x 3.0 = 1800 N m
1 mark: R_right = 300 N
2 marks: R_left + R_right = 750 N
1 mark: R_left = 450 N
2 marks: (b)(iii) The point through which the resultant weight of a body appears to act

questions.topic: Refraction of light at plane surfaces
questions.stem:
A student traced the outline ABCD of a rectangular glass block on a sheet of paper fixed to a drawing board. A normal was drawn at a point O on AB, and pins were used to trace rays incident at O at angles i to the normal. For each angle of incidence the corresponding angle of refraction r inside the block was measured with a protractor. The readings were: i/degrees: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70; r/degrees: 13.0, 19.0, 25.0, 30.5, 34.5, 38.5.
(a)(i) Find sin i and sin r for each pair, to 3 decimal places. [4 marks]
(ii) A graph of sin i (vertical axis) against sin r (horizontal axis) gives a straight line through (0.200, 0.307) and (0.600, 0.910). Calculate its slope. [3 marks]
(iii) What physical quantity does the slope represent? [1 mark]
(iv) Use your result to calculate the critical angle for the glass. [3 marks]
(v) State two precautions taken to obtain accurate results with the pins. [2 marks]
(b)(i) State Snell's law. [2 marks]
(ii) Explain, with reference to speed, why light bends towards the normal on entering glass from air. [2 marks]
(iii) The speed of light in air is 3.0 x 10^8 m s^-1. Calculate the speed of light in the glass, using your value from (a)(ii). [3 marks]
(iv) State two conditions necessary for total internal reflection. [2 marks]
(v) Name one application of total internal reflection. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) sin i: 0.342, 0.500, 0.643, 0.766, 0.866, 0.940
2 marks: sin r: 0.225, 0.326, 0.423, 0.508, 0.566, 0.623 (deduct 1 mark per two wrong values)
1 mark: (a)(ii) slope = (0.910 - 0.307)/(0.600 - 0.200)
2 marks: = 1.51 (accept 1.45 to 1.60)
1 mark: (a)(iii) The refractive index of the glass (from air to glass)
1 mark: (a)(iv) sin C = 1/n
1 mark: = 1/1.51 = 0.663
1 mark: C = 41.6 degrees
2 marks: (a)(v) Any two: pins placed upright and well separated (at least 6 cm apart); viewed the bases of the pins when aligning; pins aligned with eye at the level of the board; outline of block traced accurately and block not moved (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) For two given media, the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant (refractive index)
2 marks: (b)(ii) Light travels more slowly in glass than in air, so the wavefront is slowed on entering and the ray is deviated towards the normal
1 mark: (b)(iii) v = c/n
2 marks: = 3.0 x 10^8/1.51 = 1.99 x 10^8 m s^-1
2 marks: (b)(iv) Light travels from an optically denser to a less dense medium; the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle (1 mark each)
3 marks: (b)(v) Any one, with brief explanation: optical fibres (endoscopes/telecommunication); prism periscopes and binoculars; sparkling of diamonds; mirages (1 mark for naming, 2 marks for explanation)

questions.topic: Refraction of light at curved surfaces
questions.stem:
In an experiment to determine the focal length f of a converging lens, an illuminated object was placed at a distance u from the lens and a white screen was moved until a sharp image was obtained at a distance v from the lens. The readings were: u/cm: 15.0, 20.0, 25.0, 30.0, 35.0, 40.0; v/cm: 60.2, 29.9, 23.1, 19.9, 18.3, 17.1.
(a)(i) Calculate 1/u and 1/v for each pair, to 4 decimal places. [4 marks]
(ii) A graph of 1/v (vertical axis) against 1/u (horizontal axis) is a straight line through (0.0250 cm^-1, 0.0584 cm^-1) and (0.0650 cm^-1, 0.0183 cm^-1). Calculate the slope and the intercept on the 1/v axis. [4 marks]
(iii) Calculate the intercept on the 1/u axis. [2 marks]
(iv) Using the lens formula, find f from each intercept and hence the mean value of f. [4 marks]
(v) State two precautions taken in this experiment. [2 marks]
(b)(i) Explain why no image could be focused on the screen when the object was 10 cm from this lens. [2 marks]
(ii) Calculate the power of the lens using your mean f. [2 marks]
(iii) State two uses of converging lenses. [2 marks]
(iv) Using your mean f, calculate the magnification when u = 18.0 cm. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) 1/u: 0.0667, 0.0500, 0.0400, 0.0333, 0.0286, 0.0250 cm^-1
2 marks: 1/v: 0.0166, 0.0334, 0.0433, 0.0503, 0.0546, 0.0585 cm^-1 (deduct 1 mark per two wrong values)
2 marks: (a)(ii) slope = (0.0183 - 0.0584)/(0.0650 - 0.0250) = -1.00 (about -1)
2 marks: Intercept on 1/v axis = 0.0584 - (-1.00)(0.0250) = 0.0835 cm^-1
2 marks: (a)(iii) Intercept on 1/u axis = -c/slope = 0.0833 cm^-1
1 mark: (a)(iv) When 1/u = 0, 1/v = 1/f: f = 1/0.0835 = 12.0 cm
1 mark: When 1/v = 0, 1/u = 1/f: f = 1/0.0833 = 12.0 cm
2 marks: Mean f = 12.0 cm (accept 11.5 to 12.5 cm)
2 marks: (a)(v) Any two: lens, object and screen centres in a straight line (coaxial); sharp image obtained by moving screen to and fro; distances measured to the optical centre of the lens; experiment done in a darkened room; avoided parallax in reading the rule (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) The object was inside the focal length (u < f), so the image is virtual and cannot be formed on a screen
1 mark: (b)(ii) P = 1/f (in m) = 1/0.120
1 mark: = 8.3 D
2 marks: (b)(iii) Any two: magnifying glass; camera; projector; spectacles for long sight; microscope/telescope objective (1 mark each)
1 mark: (b)(iv) 1/v = 1/12.0 - 1/18.0, v = 36.0 cm
2 marks: m = v/u = 2.00

questions.topic: Reflection of light at curved surfaces
questions.stem:
A concave mirror was mounted vertically facing an illuminated cross-wire object. For various object distances u, a screen was adjusted until a sharp image was obtained at a distance v from the mirror. The readings were: u/cm: 14.0, 16.0, 18.0, 20.0, 25.0, 30.0; v/cm: 35.1, 26.6, 22.5, 19.9, 16.7, 15.0.
(a)(i) Calculate the magnification m = v/u for each pair, to 2 decimal places. [3 marks]
(ii) A graph of m (vertical axis) against v (horizontal axis) is a straight line through (15.0 cm, 0.50) and (35.0 cm, 2.50). Calculate the slope. [3 marks]
(iii) Given that m = v/f - 1, determine the focal length f of the mirror from the slope. [3 marks]
(iv) Calculate the intercept on the m axis and comment on its value. [3 marks]
(v) State two precautions taken in the experiment. [2 marks]
(b)(i) Define the radius of curvature of a concave mirror and state its relation to f. [2 marks]
(ii) An object 2.0 cm tall is placed 6.0 cm from this mirror. Using your value of f, calculate the image distance and image height, and state the nature of the image. [6 marks]
(iii) Give one use of a concave mirror. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) m: 2.51, 1.66, 1.25, 0.99, 0.67, 0.50 (deduct 1 mark for each wrong value)
1 mark: (a)(ii) slope = (2.50 - 0.50)/(35.0 - 15.0)
2 marks: = 0.1000 cm^-1
1 mark: (a)(iii) slope = 1/f
2 marks: f = 1/0.1000 = 10.0 cm (accept 9.5 to 10.5 cm)
2 marks: (a)(iv) intercept = 0.50 - 0.1000 x 15.0 = -1.00
1 mark: Close to -1, as predicted by m = v/f - 1
2 marks: (a)(v) Any two: object, mirror and screen centres in line; sharp image located by moving screen to and fro; distances measured from the pole of the mirror; darkened room; avoid parallax in reading the rule (1 mark each)
1 mark: (b)(i) The radius of the sphere of which the mirror is a part (distance from pole to centre of curvature)
1 mark: r = 2f
2 marks: (b)(ii) 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = 1/10.0 - 1/6.0, v = -15.0 cm
2 marks: m = |v|/u = 2.50; image height = 5.0 cm
2 marks: Image is virtual, upright and magnified (behind the mirror)
3 marks: (b)(iii) Any one with explanation: shaving/make-up mirror (magnified upright image when close); reflector in torch/headlamp (lamp at focus gives parallel beam); dentist's mirror; solar concentrator (1 mark for use, 2 marks for explanation)
questions.explanation: m values 2.51, 1.66, 1.25, 0.99, 0.67, 0.50; slope 0.1000 cm^-1 = 1/f so f = 10.0 cm; intercept -1.00 (about -1). At u = 6.0 cm, v = -15.0 cm (virtual), image 5.0 cm tall.

questions.stem:
In an experiment to determine the resistivity of the material of a wire of diameter 0.40 mm, a length l of the wire was connected in series with an accumulator, an ammeter, a key and a rheostat, and a voltmeter was connected across the length l. For each length, the current I and potential difference V were recorded: l/cm: 20.0, 40.0, 60.0, 80.0, 100.0; V/V: 1.05, 1.81, 2.37, 2.79, 3.16; I/A: 0.60, 0.52, 0.45, 0.40, 0.36.
(a)(i) Calculate the resistance R = V/I for each length, to 2 decimal places. [3 marks]
(ii) A graph of R (vertical axis) against l (horizontal axis) is a straight line through (20.0 cm, 1.74 ohms) and (100.0 cm, 8.76 ohms). Calculate the slope in ohm m^-1. [3 marks]
(iii) Calculate the cross-sectional area of the wire (pi = 3.142). [2 marks]
(iv) Determine the resistivity of the material of the wire. [3 marks]
(v) Why was the key opened between readings? [2 marks]
(vi) State one other precaution. [1 mark]
(b)(i) Define resistivity and state its S.I. unit. [2 marks]
(ii) State two factors other than length on which the resistance of a wire depends. [2 marks]
(iii) A 2.0 m length of this wire is connected across a 3.0 V cell of negligible internal resistance. Using your slope, calculate the current and the power dissipated. [5 marks]
(iv) Why is nichrome used in heating elements? [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) R: 1.75, 3.48, 5.27, 6.97, 8.78 ohms (deduct 1 mark for each wrong value)
1 mark: (a)(ii) slope = (8.76 - 1.74)/(100.0 - 20.0) = 0.0877 ohm cm^-1
2 marks: = 8.77 ohm m^-1
1 mark: (a)(iii) A = pi d^2/4 = 3.142 x (0.40 x 10^-3)^2/4
1 mark: = 1.257 x 10^-7 m^2
1 mark: (a)(iv) rho = slope x A (since R = rho l/A)
2 marks: = 8.77 x 1.257 x 10^-7 = 1.10 x 10^-6 ohm m
2 marks: (a)(v) To prevent the wire heating up, since a rise in temperature changes its resistance (and to save the accumulator)
1 mark: (a)(vi) Any one: clean wire contacts/tight connections; avoid parallax in reading meters; diameter measured at several points with a micrometer screw gauge
1 mark: (b)(i) Resistivity is the resistance of a conductor of unit length and unit cross-sectional area (rho = RA/l)
1 mark: Unit: ohm metre
2 marks: (b)(ii) Cross-sectional area (thickness); nature of material; temperature (any two, 1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(iii) R = 8.77 x 2.0 = 17.55 ohms
1 mark: I = 3.0/17.55 = 0.17 A
2 marks: P = V I = 3.0 x 0.17 = 0.51 W
2 marks: (b)(iv) It has a high resistivity and a high melting point, and does not oxidise readily when red hot
questions.explanation: R values 1.75, 3.48, 5.27, 6.97, 8.78 ohms; slope 8.77 ohm m^-1; A = 1.257 x 10^-7 m^2; resistivity = 1.10 x 10^-6 ohm m (nichrome-like). 2.0 m of wire on 3.0 V draws 0.17 A, dissipating 0.51 W.

questions.topic: Measurement of electric current, p.d., resistance, e.m.f. and internal resistance of a cell
questions.stem:
A dry cell was connected in series with an ammeter, a key and a rheostat, and a high-resistance voltmeter was connected across the terminals of the cell. The rheostat was adjusted to give different currents I and the terminal potential difference V was recorded each time: I/A: 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.70; V/V: 1.40, 1.32, 1.25, 1.17, 1.10, 1.02.
(a)(i) Calculate the external resistance R = V/I for each reading, to 2 decimal places. [3 marks]
(ii) A graph of V (vertical axis) against I (horizontal axis) gives a straight line through (0.20 A, 1.399 V) and (0.70 A, 1.021 V). Calculate its slope. [3 marks]
(iii) Using V = E - Ir, determine the internal resistance r of the cell. [2 marks]
(iv) Determine the e.m.f. E of the cell from the intercept on the V axis. [3 marks]
(v) State two precautions taken in this experiment. [2 marks]
(b)(i) Distinguish between the e.m.f. of a cell and its terminal potential difference. [2 marks]
(ii) Using your values of E and r, calculate the current when the cell is short-circuited. [2 marks]
(iii) Using your values of E and r, calculate the power delivered to an external resistor of 2.0 ohms. [4 marks]
(iv) State two ways of reducing the internal resistance of a battery. [2 marks]
(v) Why should a dry cell not be short-circuited? [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) R: 7.00, 4.40, 3.12, 2.34, 1.83, 1.46 ohms (deduct 1 mark for each wrong value)
1 mark: (a)(ii) slope = (1.021 - 1.399)/(0.70 - 0.20)
2 marks: = -0.756 V A^-1 (ohms)
2 marks: (a)(iii) r = -slope = 0.76 ohm (accept 0.70 to 0.85 ohm)
1 mark: (a)(iv) At I = 0, V = E
2 marks: E = 1.399 + 0.756 x 0.20 = 1.55 V (accept 1.50 to 1.60 V)
2 marks: (a)(v) Any two: key opened between readings to avoid running down the cell; tight, clean connections; meters read at eye level avoiding parallax; pointer adjusted to zero before use (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) The e.m.f. is the p.d. across the terminals when no current is drawn (open circuit); terminal p.d. is the p.d. when the cell delivers current and is less than the e.m.f. by Ir
1 mark: (b)(ii) I = E/r
1 mark: = 1.55/0.76 = 2.1 A
2 marks: (b)(iii) I = E/(R + r) = 1.55/(2.0 + 0.76) = 0.562 A
2 marks: P = I^2 R = 0.562^2 x 2.0 = 0.63 W
2 marks: (b)(iv) Connect cells in parallel; use plates of larger area / plates closer together; keep electrolyte at proper concentration (any two)
2 marks: (b)(v) A very large current flows, the cell overheats and is quickly exhausted/damaged
questions.explanation: R values 7.00, 4.40, 3.12, 2.34, 1.83, 1.46 ohms. Slope -0.756 ohm gives r = 0.76 ohm; intercept E = 1.55 V. Short-circuit current 2.1 A; power in 2.0 ohm = 0.63 W.

questions.stem:
A lagged copper calorimeter of negligible heat capacity contains 0.40 kg of a liquid (kerosene). An immersion heater, through which a steady current of 3.0 A flows from a 12.0 V supply, is placed in the liquid. The liquid is stirred and its temperature theta recorded every minute: t/s: 0, 60, 120, 180, 240, 300; theta/degrees C: 27.0, 29.6, 32.1, 34.7, 37.2, 39.9.
(a)(i) Calculate the rise in temperature (theta - 27.0) for each reading. [3 marks]
(ii) A graph of theta (vertical axis) against t (horizontal axis) gives a straight line through (0 s, 27.0 degrees C) and (300 s, 39.8 degrees C). Calculate its slope. [3 marks]
(iii) Calculate the power of the heater. [2 marks]
(iv) Assuming no heat loss, determine the specific heat capacity of the liquid. [4 marks]
(v) Why was the liquid stirred continuously? [1 mark]
(vi) State two precautions to reduce heat losses. [2 marks]
(b)(i) Define specific heat capacity. [2 marks]
(ii) State one reason why the value obtained would be higher than the true value. [2 marks]
(iii) The same heater is placed in 0.40 kg of water (c = 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1) at 27.0 degrees C. Calculate the time it would take to raise the temperature of the water to 39.8 degrees C. [4 marks]
(iv) Explain why water is used as a coolant in car radiators. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Rise: 0.0, 2.6, 5.1, 7.7, 10.2, 12.9 degrees C (deduct 1 mark for each wrong value)
1 mark: (a)(ii) slope = (39.8 - 27.0)/(300 - 0)
2 marks: = 0.0427 K s^-1
1 mark: (a)(iii) P = IV = 3.0 x 12.0
1 mark: = 36 W
2 marks: (a)(iv) Power = m c (rate of rise): 36 = 0.40 x c x slope
2 marks: c = 36/(0.40 x 0.0427) = 2109 J kg^-1 K^-1 (accept 2000 to 2200)
1 mark: (a)(v) To distribute heat evenly so that the thermometer reads the uniform temperature of the liquid
2 marks: (a)(vi) Any two: lagging the calorimeter; using a lid; polishing the outside of the calorimeter; keeping the temperature rise small/starting below room temperature (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) The quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of unit mass (1 kg) of a substance by 1 K
2 marks: (b)(ii) Some heat is lost to the surroundings (and calorimeter), so more energy appears to be needed per kelvin than is really absorbed by the liquid
2 marks: (b)(iii) Q = mc Delta theta = 0.40 x 4200 x 12.8 = 21 504 J
2 marks: t = Q/P = 21 504/36 = 597 s
2 marks: (b)(iv) Water has a high specific heat capacity, so it absorbs much heat from the engine with only a small rise in temperature
questions.explanation: Slope 0.0427 K s^-1; heater power 36 W; c = 36/(0.40 x slope) = 2109 J kg^-1 K^-1, typical of kerosene. Water needs 21 504 J, taking 597 s.

questions.topic: Vibration of air in pipes: open and closed pipes
questions.stem:
A long glass tube, open at both ends, is clamped vertically with its lower end in a tall jar of water. A sounding tuning fork of frequency f is held over the top of the tube and the tube is raised gradually until the first loud resonance is heard. The length l of the air column above the water is then measured. The readings for six tuning forks were: f/Hz: 256, 288, 320, 384, 426, 512; l/cm: 32.1, 28.2, 25.4, 20.9, 18.9, 15.4.
(a)(i) Calculate 1/f for each fork, to 5 decimal places. [3 marks]
(ii) A graph of l (vertical axis) against 1/f (horizontal axis) is a straight line through (0.00200 s, 15.8 cm) and (0.00390 s, 31.9 cm). Calculate its slope in m s^-1. [3 marks]
(iii) Given that l = v/(4f) - c, where c is the end correction, determine the speed of sound v. [3 marks]
(iv) Determine the end correction c from the intercept. [3 marks]
(v) State two precautions taken in this experiment. [2 marks]
(b)(i) Explain why a loud sound is heard at resonance. [2 marks]
(ii) Calculate the length of air column at which the second resonance would be heard with the 512 Hz fork, using your values of v and c. [3 marks]
(iii) State two factors that affect the speed of sound in air. [2 marks]
(iv) Distinguish between a stationary wave and a progressive wave. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) 1/f: 0.00391, 0.00347, 0.00313, 0.00260, 0.00235, 0.00195 s (deduct 1 mark for each wrong value)
1 mark: (a)(ii) slope = (31.9 - 15.8)/(0.00390 - 0.00200) = 8474 cm s^-1
2 marks: = 84.7 m s^-1
1 mark: (a)(iii) slope = v/4
2 marks: v = 4 x 84.7 = 339 m s^-1 (accept 335 to 350)
1 mark: (a)(iv) The intercept on the l axis is -c
2 marks: intercept = 15.8 - 8474 x 0.00200 = -1.15 cm, so c = 1.15 cm
2 marks: (a)(v) Any two: fork struck on a rubber pad, not a hard surface; fork held horizontally just above the tube without touching it; tube raised slowly and loudest point located by moving up and down; meniscus read at eye level; avoided parallax (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) The natural frequency of the air column equals the frequency of the fork, so the air column vibrates with maximum amplitude (stationary wave formed)
1 mark: (b)(ii) l2 + c = 3v/(4f)
2 marks: l2 = 3 x 339/(4 x 512) - 0.0115 = 0.485 m
2 marks: (b)(iii) Any two: temperature; humidity; wind (pressure has no effect at constant temperature) (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(iv) A progressive wave transfers energy from the source and all particles have the same amplitude
2 marks: A stationary wave does not transfer energy; it has nodes and antinodes with amplitude varying from zero to maximum
questions.explanation: 1/f values 0.00391, 0.00347, 0.00313, 0.00260, 0.00235, 0.00195 s; slope 84.7 m s^-1 = v/4, v = 339 m s^-1; end correction 1.15 cm. Second resonance with 512 Hz at 0.485 m.

questions.stem:
A flat-bottomed test tube containing some sand was floated upright in water (density 1.00 g cm^-3) in a measuring cylinder. Lead shots of total mass m were added in turn and the depth h of the bottom of the tube below the water surface was measured each time: m/g: 5.0, 10.0, 15.0, 20.0, 25.0, 30.0; h/cm: 7.0, 8.6, 10.4, 12.0, 13.6, 15.3.
(a)(i) A graph of h (vertical axis) against m (horizontal axis) is a straight line through (5.0 g, 7.00 cm) and (30.0 g, 15.30 cm). Calculate its slope. [3 marks]
(ii) Calculate the intercept on the h axis. [2 marks]
(iii) Using the law of flotation, show that h = m/(A rho) + M/(A rho), where A is the cross-sectional area of the tube, rho the density of water and M the mass of the tube and sand. [3 marks]
(iv) Use your slope to determine A. [2 marks]
(v) Use the intercept to determine M. [3 marks]
(vi) Why was sand put in the tube? [1 mark]
(vii) State two precautions taken. [2 marks]
(b)(i) State the law of flotation. [2 marks]
(ii) With 20.0 g of shots, the tube was transferred to brine and floated with 10.6 cm immersed. Using your values of A and M, calculate the density of the brine. [4 marks]
(iii) Name an instrument that uses this principle and state one use. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a)(i) slope = (15.30 - 7.00)/(30.0 - 5.0)
2 marks: = 0.332 cm g^-1
2 marks: (a)(ii) intercept = 7.00 - 0.332 x 5.0 = 5.34 cm
1 mark: (a)(iii) Floating: weight of tube + sand + shots = weight of water displaced
1 mark: (M + m) g = A h rho g
1 mark: h = m/(A rho) + M/(A rho)
2 marks: (a)(iv) slope = 1/(A rho); A = 1/(0.332 x 1.00) = 3.01 cm^2
1 mark: (a)(v) intercept = M/(A rho)
2 marks: M = 5.34 x 3.01 x 1.00 = 16.1 g
1 mark: (a)(vi) To lower the centre of gravity so the tube floats upright (stable)
2 marks: (a)(vii) Any two: tube floated freely without touching the sides; depth read at eye level/bottom of meniscus; shots added gently; tube dried before reading (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) A floating body displaces its own weight of the fluid in which it floats
2 marks: (b)(ii) Total mass = 16.1 + 20.0 = 36.1 g = A h rho_b
2 marks: rho_b = 36.1/(3.01 x 10.6) = 1.13 g cm^-3
1 mark: (b)(iii) Hydrometer
2 marks: Used to measure the relative density of liquids, e.g. testing the acid in a car battery, or milk and palm wine for dilution
questions.explanation: Slope 0.332 cm g^-1 = 1/(A rho), so A = 3.01 cm^2; intercept 5.34 cm gives M = 16.1 g. In brine: rho = 36.1/(3.01 x 10.6) = 1.13 g cm^-3.

questions.stem:
In an experiment to verify Boyle's law, air was trapped in a glass tube by a column of oil connected to a pressure gauge and a pump. The temperature was kept constant. For different pressures p, the volume V of the trapped air was recorded: p/kPa: 100, 120, 140, 160, 180, 200; V/cm^3: 30.1, 25.0, 21.4, 18.7, 16.7, 15.0.
(a)(i) Calculate 1/p (in kPa^-1) for each reading, to 5 decimal places. [3 marks]
(ii) Calculate the product pV for each reading. [3 marks]
(iii) A graph of V (vertical axis) against 1/p (horizontal axis) is a straight line through (0.00500 kPa^-1, 15.0 cm^3) and (0.01000 kPa^-1, 30.1 cm^3). Calculate its slope. [3 marks]
(iv) What do the results of (ii) and (iii) show? [2 marks]
(v) Why was a short time allowed after each change of pressure before reading the volume? [2 marks]
(vi) State one other precaution. [1 mark]
(b)(i) State Boyle's law. [2 marks]
(ii) Use your slope to find the volume of the air at a pressure of 250 kPa. [2 marks]
(iii) Explain Boyle's law using the kinetic theory of gases. [3 marks]
(iv) A bubble of gas of volume 2.0 cm^3 is released at the bottom of a lake where the total pressure is 300 kPa. Calculate its volume just below the surface where the pressure is 100 kPa, assuming constant temperature. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) 1/p: 0.01000, 0.00833, 0.00714, 0.00625, 0.00556, 0.00500 kPa^-1 (deduct 1 mark for each wrong value)
3 marks: (a)(ii) pV: 3010, 3000, 2996, 2992, 3006, 3000 kPa cm^3 (deduct 1 mark for each wrong value)
1 mark: (a)(iii) slope = (30.1 - 15.0)/(0.01000 - 0.00500)
2 marks: = 3020 kPa cm^3
2 marks: (a)(iv) pV is constant (about 3000 kPa cm^3) and V is proportional to 1/p: the gas obeys Boyle's law
